sources.note: Bibliographic only. Glottolog: zero descriptive refs; Glottolog's most extensive description = Bradbury 1968 comparative Edo wordlists (a wordlist or less); page lists Lewis 2013 and Ethnologue 2025 only. Ethnologue 2019: alternate names Ekpeshe, Ikpeshe; North-Central > Ghotuo-Uneme-Yekhee; no language resources. Wikipedia cites only Lewis 2015 (USEM), Agheyisi 1984 (word, minority-language list) and Ekwukoma & Odiagbe 2025. ASJP holds a Bradbury-1968-based wordlist, no prosody.

sources.citation: Lewis, Demola. 2015. Geography and Lexical Feature Diffusion in Northwestern Edo. USEM Journal of Languages, Linguistics and Literature (Univ. of Uyo) 7: 124-147.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Lexical diffusion study built on 500-item wordlists elicited in 36 villages; Ikpeshi appears only as a member of lexical sets (items (1) sleep, (14)-(18), (24) person, (26) see/big/old) and in sec. 9 'Orle Diffusion Belt' ('the valley settlements of Okpella, North Ibie, Atte, Ikpeshi, Ososo.. have exclusive vocabulary stemming from diffusion', p.138). No phonological description, no tone or stress statement; the word forms are not rendered in the text layer.

sources.citation: Egbokhare, Francis O. 2011. The Sound of Meaning. Inaugural lecture, University of Ibadan.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Ikpeshi phonology. Ikpeshi is a 'one-village community' (p.68); on mutual intelligibility it belongs to the Akoko-Edo group 'Atte Ikpeshi-Enwan-Okpilla-North Ibie (NWE)' (p.68); the Northern Edo project recorded narrative tapes at Ikpeshi, which 'have been transcribed and translated', and collected an Ibadan-400 wordlist for all NE communities (pp.71-72) -- all unpublished. Table 8 on NCE/NWE tone systems has no Ikpeshi row; stress is not mentioned.

sources.note: Nothing for Ikpeshi. The language is named once, in the footnote to the ethnic list on pp.10-11: 'The following clans, not named in the list above, are most likely North-Central Edoid peoples: Xososo, Ate (Atte), Ikpeshi, Sasaru, and Enwan, all of Akoko-Edo'. No Ikpeshi data in the comparative phonology or lexicon; family-wide chapters treat tone, not stress.
